description: On October 12, 1492, Christopher Columbus reached an island in the Bahamas that he believed was Japan. One navigational error opened the age of globalization.

hero.hook: He was looking for Asia. He ran into a continent Europe had forgotten.

blocks.text: On **October 12, 1492**, after more than two months on the Atlantic, a sailor on the Pinta shouted “Land!” **Christopher Columbus**, a Genoese in the service of Spain, landed on an island in the Bahamas and named it San Salvador. He was certain he had reached Asia.

That mistake would tie two hemispheres together. Carried by the momentum of the [[Spanish Reconquista (1492)]], the recapture of Granada from the Muslims that same year, the voyage marked for Europe the passage from the Middle Ages to the modern era.

Columbus was not trying to prove that the Earth is round. [[Eratosthenes]], a Greek scholar of the 3rd century BC, had already measured it. The real goal was economic: reach the spices and silk of Asia by sailing west, without dealing with the Ottomans, who controlled the eastern routes.

blocks.caption: Christopher Columbus, the Genoese navigator in the service of the Catholic Monarchs

blocks.text: His error was to underestimate the size of the Earth. He put Japan **4,500 km** from the Canary Islands, when the real distance is closer to **20,000**. Portugal turned him down. Isabella of Castile, queen of Spain, said yes. A contract, the [[Capitulations of Santa Fe]], made him an admiral and a viceroy with **10%** of the profits.
Columbus wrote that he had seen mermaids in the Caribbean. They were manatees. He noted, with some disappointment, that they were far less beautiful than the legends promised.

sections.title: A route west, and a very large mistake

blocks.text: On **August 3, 1492**, three ships left Palos in Spain: the **Pinta**, the **Niña**, and the **Santa María**. Thanks to the [[Pinzón]] family, wealthy local shipowners, the crew of **90 men** was experienced. The crossing took **70 days**. Columbus kept two logbooks, one true and one falsified, to keep his sailors calm.

blocks.caption: The Santa María, flagship of the 1492 expedition

blocks.text: On **October 12**, he met the [[Taínos]], the native people of the Greater Antilles. Convinced he was in the Indies, he called them “Indians.” He noted their gold and their apparent meekness. The colonial gaze was already there.
The Niña was really called *Santa Clara*. The Santa María was nicknamed *La Gallega*, because she was built in Galicia.

The arrival of the Europeans set off the **Columbian Exchange**, a huge transfer of plants, animals, and diseases between the two worlds. Eastward to Europe: potato, corn, tomato, cocoa, tobacco. Westward to America: wheat, sugar, coffee, horses, cattle. Meals and landscapes on both sides changed forever.

The price was terrible. Smallpox, measles, and influenza killed **50% to 90%** of the native population within a century. On the diplomatic front, Spain and Portugal split the globe between them with the [[Treaty of Tordesillas (1494)]], without consulting anyone.

events.detail: Spain and Portugal divide the world between them.
events.title: Tordesillas

blocks.text: Columbus died in **1506** without ever admitting what he had found. It was [[Amerigo Vespucci]], a Florentine navigator, who understood that this was a “Mundus Novus,” a New World. In **1507**, the mapmaker Waldseemüller named the continent **America**. The Florentine's first name went onto the map of the world.

A brutal administrator on Hispaniola, today Haiti and the Dominican Republic, Columbus was eventually sent home in chains. Beyond the man, **1492** opened the age of globalization. American silver poured in, and the center of trade slid from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic. Europe became the hinge of a system spanning four continents.
Columbus died convinced he had reached Asia. His mistake joined two hemispheres and set off a biological, economic, and human upheaval that could not be undone.
